papers.title: Native, Memory-Bounded Conversion of Mass Spectrometry Imaging Data into the SpatialData Ecosystem
papers.summary: This paper presents a software tool that converts mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) data into the SpatialData format in a memory-efficient, 'native' way. The conversion is designed to handle large imaging datasets without requiring excessive RAM, enabling scalability. This allows MSI data to be integrated alongside other spatial omics modalities within a unified computational ecosystem.
papers.why: Since the project involves integrating spatial metabolomics with spatial transcriptomics for studying mitophagy and perineuronal nets in neurons, a tool that interoperably converts MS imaging data into a common spatial data framework directly supports multi-omic data integration workflows.
papers.figure: A schematic diagram showing the data conversion pipeline from raw MSI formats into SpatialData objects, including memory usage benchmarks.

papers.title: SpatialTRACE predicts anatomical axes and regions in spatial transcriptomics and microscopy
papers.summary: SpatialTRACE is a computational tool designed to predict anatomical axes and regional identity directly from spatial transcriptomics and microscopy data. It likely uses machine learning to map molecular and spatial patterns onto known brain anatomy, helping researchers automatically annotate tissue sections. This could streamline the process of aligning gene expression or imaging data to standardized brain atlases.
papers.why: This tool could help automatically map spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics data from brain sections onto anatomical regions, supporting precise localization of interneurons and perineuronal nets across brain areas in this PhD project.

papers.title: AI-driven transcriptomics for neurodegenerative disease research: A systematic review.
papers.summary: This paper is a systematic review that surveys how artificial intelligence and machine learning methods have been applied to transcriptomic data in the context of neurodegenerative disease research. It likely catalogs the types of AI models used (e.g., deep learning, clustering, classification algorithms), the transcriptomic data types involved (bulk, single-cell, spatial), and the diseases studied (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, etc.). Since it is a review without new experimental data, it probably synthesizes trends, challenges, and gaps in current AI-transcriptomics approaches rather than presenting a single figure or dataset.
papers.why: This review could help identify state-of-the-art AI/deep learning approaches for analyzing spatial transcriptomics data relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons and interneurons within neurodegenerative contexts.

papers.title: The neuroprotective mechanism of baicalein related to mitophagy mediated by MAPK1/RSK1 in a murine model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how baicalein, a natural flavonoid compound, protects brain neurons in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. The protective effect appears to work through mitophagy, a process where damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared from cells, and this process is regulated by a signaling pathway involving MAPK1 and RSK1 proteins. The findings suggest a potential therapeutic strategy for Parkinson's disease by targeting this specific mitophagy-regulating pathway.
papers.why: This directly relates to mitophagy mechanisms in neurons and could inform understanding of how disrupted mitochondrial quality control contributes to neurodegeneration, relevant background for studying mitophagy/autophagy dysfunction in interneurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing colocalization of mitophagy markers (e.g., LC3, PINK1/Parkin) with mitochondria in neurons, alongside MAPK1/RSK1 pathway activation status across treatment groups.

papers.title: Enabling subcellular DESI-MSI for broad adoption: Acquisition, analysis, and application
papers.summary: This paper describes methods to make desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging (DESI-MSI) work at subcellular resolution in a way that other labs can adopt more easily. It covers improvements in how the data is acquired, how it is processed and analyzed, and demonstrates practical applications of the technique. The goal is to lower the technical barrier so subcellular-resolution spatial metabolomics becomes more widely usable.
papers.why: High-resolution spatial metabolomics tools like this could let you map metabolite and lipid signatures within individual neurons or perineuronal net microenvironments, complementing your spatial metabolomics and mitophagy work in interneurons.

papers.title: Targeting SIRT2-mediated mitophagy to enhance ferroptosis: a novel mechanism of berberine action in non-small cell lung cancer.
papers.summary: This study investigates how berberine, a natural compound, affects non-small cell lung cancer cells. The authors propose that berberine works by modulating SIRT2, a protein that regulates mitophagy (the selective degradation of damaged mitochondria). This mitophagy modulation is shown to enhance ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, suggesting a new anticancer mechanism.
papers.why: Although focused on cancer rather than neurons, this paper explores SIRT2-mediated mitophagy regulation, a mechanistic pathway potentially relevant to understanding mitophagy control mechanisms applicable to neuronal contexts.

papers.title: Mechanistic Study of SRSF1-Mediated Inhibition of Treg Cell Function via the mTORC1/ULK1 Signalling Axis Through Mitophagy in Asthma.
papers.summary: This study investigates how a protein called SRSF1 affects regulatory T cells (Tregs), which are immune cells that help control inflammation, in the context of asthma. The researchers focus on a signalling pathway called mTORC1/ULK1, which controls mitophagy—the process of clearing out damaged mitochondria within cells. They show that SRSF1 disrupts this mitophagy pathway, which impairs Treg function and may contribute to worsening asthma symptoms.
papers.why: Although this paper centers on immune cells rather than neurons, its detailed mechanistic dissection of mTORC1/ULK1-mediated mitophagy regulation offers a transferable signalling framework that could inform studies of mitophagy dysregulation in neurons and interneurons within the brain.
